First, a preface and a warning:

When you've read one how-to-write-a-novel-everyone-will-buy book, you've read them all. This is my bitter experience from a lot of pages turned on such texts. When you cut down every how-to book about writing to size, be it Stephen King's On Writing down to the Plotto plot wheel, the only answer they really give to the question "How do I write a novel that people will read?" is "Write one." About the best book I've read on the construction of fiction is Robert McKee's Story, and he teaches screenplay, so the translation is not ideal. It's also a better book because it dares to be a bit more objective than most about the actual elements of stories, but this is not a review for it, so I'll leave it aside.

This frustration doesn't get any better when you turn to how-to books by people who ought to be able to tell you how writing is done. You'd think Stephen King could tell you a bit about how to write a book. But his On Writing is one of the worst books on writing that's ever been published. To be fair, King gives you fair warning right up front in the fucking title: the book is subtitled "A Memoir of the Craft", not "A How-To book." King's advice on writing really comes down to: (1) Omit adverbs (2) Don't do drugs, maaaaaaan.

But let's not be hard on the old bastard. He also admits in the book that very few writers have any idea how their stories actually work. And it's not like many of his contemporaries do much better in this department. I defy any first-time or apprentice writer to read John Gardner's The Art of Fiction and not end the book wanting to ram Gardner's pipe up his arsehole. As they get older, career novelists seem to get more and more Zen and, worse still, elitist about what they do. Try going through the (free) "On Writing" articles on Dan Simmons' website and you will be explicitly directed to Zen principles as a part of your "education". No matter which author it is telling you how to write a book, if it's not something you've already been told or searched up on the Internet, beware.

Second warning: even less helpful is the wastepaper-basket publishing that comes out of the magazine Writer's Digest. These guys slaughter more trees giving would-be authors mediocre advice than books they help publish.

Novel Shortcuts is out of that stable. Whitcomb at least doesn't have the bloated career behind her to warp her memories of what it was like starting out as a writer: she's only published four novels, most of which are in the "supernatural romance" genre, i.e., second rate Twilight category.

So, all of that being said, how's the book?

Patchy. And not in a good way. According to one reader on Amazon, sections of the book are outright plagiarised from other how-to books without attribution. I haven't gone to check on the veracity of that complaint personally, mainly because I'm trying not to kill myself.

Perhaps the best nuggets in the book are around brainstorming and getting yourself in the actual mindset to write. I could resonate with her suggestions around getting a "soundtrack" for the book in your head and making lists of things that need to happen in scenes, mainly because like Whitcomb I'm a person who makes lists and can get emotional from music.

The book has recommendations to read other books I recognised which are points in favour: at least she's not directing you to the wrong shit entirely. At least it has a bibliography, which non-fiction books should have. And unlike James Scott Bell who took two separate books to tell his readers what the hell the "premise" of a story was, she doesn't put different names on the elements of writing trying to make her book appear more groundbreaking than it is. (That said, her notion of "crosshairs moments" in fiction is stupid labelling. She could've just as easily said: the climax of every scene needs to be the focus of your writing in the scene.) But she's not giving you anything different to the bevy of how-to books that have been written before, or anything you couldn't figure out by writing a book and then finding a competent freelance editor to review it.

There are no shortcuts to writing a novel. The title of the book is a fiction. As with all how-to-write books, all you can really do is trawl it for something that works and forget the rest. But that does not make it worth the price of a purchase. Look for this one on torrents or photocopy it at a library. Don't encourage unhelpful writing books in a world where magazines like Writer's Digest have an incentive to keep you unsuccessful and keep buying their second-rate books.
